Jan Pribram
yan pree'bram
n. (Jan Pribram, died 1448, master of Prague and leader of the conservative Utraquist party against the Taborites)
Pribram, a Bohemian mining town, from a Slavic root for a gate or a passage; Jan, the Czech form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jan Pribram was a master of the university of Prague and for thirty years the ablest spokesman of the conservative wing of the Hussite movement. He held the Four Articles and the cup for the laity, and he held almost nothing else that the Taborites held. Against them he defended the real and substantial presence in the Supper in the received sense, the vestments and the Latin canon, prayers for the dead and the remaining ceremonies, and the proposition that the Bohemian church was a reformed part of the catholic church and not a new one. He wrote against the Taborite priests with great force and some malice, drew up lists of their errors for the use of the Catholic lords, and worked steadily for the settlement which became the Compacts of Basel—communion in both kinds conceded to Bohemia, and Bohemia returned to the obedience of Rome. He quarrelled with Rokycana, was driven from Prague and returned, and died in 1448. The dictionary enters him because he is the type of a figure who appears at every Reformation: the moderate who secures the one concession his people most want, and secures it by giving away everything else, and who sincerely believes that he has saved the movement rather than ended it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a compact as an agreement between parties; moderation as a restraint of violence, the keeping of a due mean; and compromise as a mutual agreement settling a dispute by concession.

expand to see more

COMPACT, n. [L. compactum.] An agreement; a contract between parties or nations; a covenant or convention.

MODERATION, n. [L. moderatio.] Restraint of violent passions or indulgence of appetite; the state of keeping a due mean between extremes.

COMPROMISE, n. [L. compromissum.] A mutual promise or contract of two parties in controversy, to refer their differences to arbitrators; an amicable agreement by concession.

CONCESSION, n. [L. concessio.] The act of granting or yielding; the thing yielded; acknowledgment by way of yielding a point.

OBEDIENCE, n. [L. obedientia.] Compliance with a command, prohibition or known law; submission to authority.

Modern Corruption

Prague master who defended the old ceremonies against the Taborites and worked for the Compacts, by which Bohemia kept the cup and returned to Rome.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the trade Pribram made, and it is worth stating as a principle rather than as a complaint about one man. The Compacts gave Bohemia the chalice and took back the doctrine the chalice had been a sign of; the Bohemian church kept a ceremony and lost its claim that Scripture is the judge. “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5) is the apostle's account of a very similar negotiation, and his answer to it was not an hour's concession.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary will not caricature him. His case was that Bohemia alone could not stand against Christendom, that the war had ruined the country, and that a church cut off from the catholic church would become a sect. All three were plausible and the first two were true. The answer is that the question was never whether Bohemia could stand but whether the thing it was asked to concede was the truth; and that a man who settles a doctrinal quarrel by a formula each side may read its own way has not made peace but postponed the war.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hupotage (G5292), subjection, a giving place; Greek aletheia (G225), truth.

expand to see more

Greek hupotage (G5292) — subjection, submission; “we gave place by subjection”, Galatians 2:5.

Greek aletheia (G225) — truth, that which is unconcealed; “the truth of the gospel”, Galatians 2:5.

Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to contend earnestly for; “earnestly contend for the faith”, Jude 3.

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.

Greek anathema (G331) — a thing accursed; “let him be accursed”, Galatians 1:8.

Usage

"“no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5) — the apostle's answer to a very similar negotiation."

"“earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — lists of Taborite errors drawn up for the Catholic lords."

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the rule the Compacts conceded while keeping the cup."
